claim: Open-source OCPP controller: EV charging in a block of flats without a bigger fuse.
stats: min above fuse, no load management
limit: Simulated building and cars; never run on real chargers or a real building meter.
alt: Dark chart. Top: highest phase current on a winter evening; without load management it rises far above the dashed 63 A fuse line, the dynamic controller stays just under it. Bottom: minutes above the fuse in 8 weeks for no load management, static split and the dynamic controller, with energy delivered.
post:
Twelve parking spaces want chargers, the building has a 3x63 A main fuse, and a bigger grid connection is expensive and slow.

I built an open-source OCPP 1.6J central system that measures the building and sends every charger a SetChargingProfile each minute, so that the flats plus all cars stay under the fuse. It is phase aware (single-phase cars), never gives a car less than 6 A (it pauses instead) and shares fairly by equal share, first come or departure time.

On 8 simulated weeks of a 24-flat building with 12 chargers, without load management the one-minute current was above 63 A for 3038 minutes. A static equal split (fixed reserve for the flats) was above it for 27 minutes and its worst-served session got 60 % of its request. The dynamic controller: 0 minutes above, 100 % of the requested energy delivered by departure, building peak 42 kW instead of 75 kW. Over real websockets one control cycle for up to 9 active chargers took 15 ms (median). An offline charger, a stale meter and a charger ignoring its profile are tested.

Not verified: no real charger, car or building meter yet; the building and the cars are simulated.

Which charger behaviour would you test first on real hardware?

Code: https://github.com/Usernamepersonperson/ocpp-load-managed-charging
